## What you will be able to do

::: {.mm-outcomes-wrap}
- Read a decision tree, diagnose its instability and control its complexity.
- Compare ridge, random forests, gradient boosting and support vector regression using the same folds and metric.
- Tune a whole modelling procedure with nested cross-validation while protecting a final test set.
- Use PCA to describe variation, and distinguish visual separation from predictive evidence.
- Cluster scaled observations, check stability and describe what the groups do and do not establish.
- Interpret permutation importance, partial dependence and individual prediction explanations with their limitations.
:::

## Before you start

::: {.prereq}
Complete [Chapter 2](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/index.html), especially pipelines, cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning. You should be able to explain why fitting a scaler before cross-validation leaks information, and why the best search score is not a final performance estimate. [Lab 2](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/labs/lab-02-first-ml-project.html) is useful preparation.
:::

The supervised examples reuse the five ESOL descriptors and the 80/20 split from Chapter 2. Model development happens inside the 80%; the lab opens the final 20% only after choosing the complete procedure. PCA uses breast-cancer measurements, and clustering returns to the penguins from Chapter 1. All examples run on a CPU with the existing course environment.

## A route through the chapter

Start with trees and ensembles, then compare their piecewise predictions with the smoother similarity rule of an SVM. PCA and clustering ask a different question: what structure is present when a target is unavailable? Finish with interpretation, then test your understanding in the [checkpoint](checkpoint.html) before undertaking the lab. A model that is harder to explain or slower to fit needs a practical benefit to justify that cost.
